sysd-reliab-013.title: Universally unique identifier: 128 bits, no registry
sysd-reliab-013.text:
A UUID is a 128-bit number that identifies information in computer systems and needs no central authority to be generated. It is usually written as 32 hexadecimal digits in the 8-4-4-4-12 hyphenated format. In software typically created by Microsoft it is called a GUID. Because no registration or coordination between generators is needed, independent parties can label information that ends up in the same data stores, with negligible probability of duplication. The probability is not zero, but it is close enough. For properly generated version-4 UUIDs, a duplicate within 103 trillion of them has a one-in-a-billion chance.

One catch is locality. Used as a data store's key for each row, random versions 3, 4 and 5 can hurt performance. So can the field ordering of versions 1 and 2. Reordering time-based UUIDs so the timestamp comes first averts the loss, which is the rationale for versions 6 and 7.

sysd-reliab-012.title: Snowflake ID: a timestamp, a machine and a counter in one number
sysd-reliab-012.text:
41 bits of time, 10 bits of machine, 12 bits of counter: that is the whole recipe for a Snowflake ID. It packs a timestamp, a machine ID and a sequence number into one number, a form of unique identifier used in distributed computing. Twitter created the format and uses it for tweet IDs, and Discord and Instagram have since adopted it. The timestamp counts milliseconds since a chosen epoch, the machine ID prevents clashes, and the per-machine sequence number lets several IDs be made in one millisecond. Only 63 bits vary, so the value fits in a 64-bit signed integer; the first bit is unused to keep IDs positive.

Snowflakes sort by creation time, and that time can be calculated from the ID. Objects created before or after a given date can therefore be selected by ID. A generator needs no network call to an ID service, so Snowflake IDs are fast and scalable. Implementations vary: Instagram, for example, uses 41 timestamp bits, 13 shard ID bits and 10 sequence bits.

sysd-reliab-014.title: UUID versions: time, name, random and custom layouts
sysd-reliab-014.text:
A UUID's bits can be filled in several ways. The choice decides whether the IDs sort by time, repeat from a name, or reveal when a system started. The versions fall into five families: time and node based, name hash based, random, time-ordered with random bits, and custom.

Version 1 is time-based. It holds a 60-bit timestamp counting 100-nanosecond intervals since 15 October 1582 UTC, a 48-bit node ID, usually a MAC address, and a clock sequence. The clock sequence avoids duplicates when the clock moves backwards. Versions 3 and 5 are name-based: they hash a namespace identifier, itself a UUID, with a name, using MD5 for version 3 and SHA-1 for version 5. Systems can then derive the same UUID from a name without a registry. Version 4 is made from random or pseudorandom numbers. Six bits are fixed for variant and version, leaving 122 random bits, which gives 5.3×10^36 possible version-4, variant-1 UUIDs.

Version 6 is field-compatible with version 1 but stores the timestamp from most to least significant byte for better locality in a data store. Systems without legacy version-1 UUIDs should use version 7 instead. Version 7 puts a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp in the most significant bits and fills the other 74 non-version, non-variant bits with random bits. Its UUIDs are monotonically ascending and lexically sortable, so new records land at the end of the key sequence. Random version 4 keys scatter across it and hurt performance. Version 8 is for experimental or vendor-specific use, and its uniqueness must not be assumed. Versions 1, 2, 6 and 7 expose the time of generation, so UUIDs can reveal when a system went live. The RFC calls the embedded timestamp a very small attack surface.

sysd-reliab-118.title: UUID best practices: storing, sorting and trusting them
sysd-reliab-118.text: RFC 9562 does more than define UUIDs. It advises how to generate, store, sort and protect them. Where feasible, store a UUID as its 128-bit binary value: text needs 288 bits for the same value, while binary takes less space and may be faster. Time-ordered monotonic UUIDs sort as raw bytes and give index locality because new values sit near each other. The gap from random inserts can be one order of magnitude or more. Avoid name-based UUIDs as keys, because the name input, such as a postal code or license number, can later change. Random bits should come from a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator. Do not assume UUIDs are hard to guess, and do not use them as security capabilities, identifiers whose mere possession grants access. Weigh the consequences of a collision: a duplicate log entry is low impact, but where failure is unacceptable, use as much collision resistance as the context allows. Treat UUIDs as opaque and avoid parsing them.

sysd-reliab-111.title: Count-min sketch: counting events in a tiny table
sysd-reliab-111.text: How do you count how often each event occurs in a stream when you cannot keep a counter for every kind? A count-min sketch is a probabilistic data structure that serves as a frequency table of events in a stream of data. It uses hash functions to map events to frequencies but, unlike an ordinary hash-keyed table, takes only sub-linear space. The price is that collisions make it overcount some events. The sketch is a two-dimensional array of w columns and d rows, with a hash function for each row. To record an event, each row hashes it to a column and increments that cell. A point query returns the least value among the event's cells. It never underestimates the true count, and with probability 1 − δ it overshoots by at most εN, where N is the total number of items seen. Because the sketch is linear, summing the sketches of two streams gives the same result as sketching the concatenated streams, so it is mergeable and suits distributed settings.

sysd-reliab-112.title: Merkle tree: checking big data with one root hash
sysd-reliab-112.text: Download a big file from strangers and you want to know two things: is it intact, and if not, which piece is bad? A Merkle tree, or hash tree, answers both. Each leaf is labelled with the cryptographic hash of a data block, and each inner node with the hash of its children's labels. The root hash comes from a trusted source, while the tree itself can come from any untrusted peer. A tree that does not match the root hash is damaged or fake, so another source is tried. One branch can be checked at a time, even before the whole tree has arrived. A file split into small blocks then needs only the damaged blocks downloaded again. Proving that a leaf belongs to a binary hash tree takes hashes proportional to the logarithm of the leaf count. A hash list needs the leaf count itself. Hash trees are used in ZFS, Git, Bitcoin and Ethereum, and in systems such as Cassandra, Riak and Dynamo.

sysd-reliab-010.title: HyperLogLog: counting distinct items in tiny memory
sysd-reliab-010.text: Counting exactly how many distinct items a data set holds takes memory proportional to that number, which is impractical for very large sets. HyperLogLog solves this count-distinct problem with a single pass over the data and very little memory. It estimates cardinalities well beyond 10^9 with a typical accuracy of 2% using only 1.5 kilobytes. The idea is to hash each element into a uniformly distributed random number and note the maximum number of leading zeros in their binary forms. One estimate alone has a large variance. So the hashed values are split into many subsets, the maximum is found in each, and a harmonic mean combines the results. In practice the state is an array of m registers, and the first b bits of an element's hash pick the register to update. Merging two sets takes the maximum of each pair of registers, so the algorithm parallelizes optimally. It is biased for small cardinalities, which HyperLogLog++ fixes with an empirical bias correction and a sparse register representation.

sysd-reliab-004.title: Cache filtering with a Bloom filter: skipping one-hit wonders
sysd-reliab-004.text: Nearly three-quarters of the URLs accessed from a typical web cache are one-hit-wonders, requested once and never again, so storing them wastes disk resources. The fix is to cache an object only when it is requested a second time. A Bloom filter keeps track of every URL users access, so a web object is stored only if it has been accessed before. Most one-hit-wonders are then never written to disk. The disk write workload drops, cache space is saved and hit rates rise. Akamai's servers use this to keep one-hit-wonders out of their disk caches.

sysd-reliab-002.title: Counting Bloom filter: a Bloom filter that can delete
sysd-reliab-002.text: A plain Bloom filter cannot forget; a counting Bloom filter can. It swaps each single bit of the array for a multibit counter, so a regular Bloom filter is just a counting filter with one-bit buckets. Insert increments the counters its hashes select, lookup checks that each is non-zero, and delete decrements each one. The price is space. Counters are usually 3 or 4 bits, so the filter takes 3 to 4 times more room than a static one. They must also be large enough that overflow stays rare. The table cannot be expanded, so the maximum number of keys must be known in advance.

sysd-reliab-003.title: Bloom filter alternatives: cuckoo, quotient and xor filters
sysd-reliab-003.text: A classic Bloom filter uses 1.44log2(1/ε) bits per inserted key. Any structure in the same role needs only log2(1/ε), so a Bloom filter uses 44% more space than an optimal one. Cuckoo, quotient and xor filters store short fingerprints of keys instead. A cuckoo filter keeps them in a table built by cuckoo hashing, and like a quotient filter it supports deletions and has better locality. An xor filter is more memory efficient, at 1.23log2(1/ε) bits per key, and faster than both. But it is harder to create, and its set cannot be modified afterwards.

sysd-reliab-011.title: Quadtree types: regions, points, lines and curves
sysd-reliab-011.text: Quadtrees are classified by the kind of data they hold, such as areas, points, lines and curves. They are also classified by whether the tree's shape depends on the order data is added. A region quadtree splits a region into four equal quadrants and so on. A point quadtree adapts a binary tree to two-dimensional points, with every subdivision centered on a point. It usually runs in O(log n) time, though k-d trees have surpassed it. A point-region quadtree stores a list of points in each leaf cell. Like the point quadtree, it can grow to linear height on a bad set of points.

sysd-reliab-009.title: Limits of geohash proximity search: where neighbors look far apart
sysd-reliab-009.text: Geohashes that share a long prefix are close together, but the reverse is not guaranteed: two nearby points can have a short or no shared prefix. Close points on opposite sides of the 180 degree meridian, near the poles, or either side of the Equator or Greenwich meridian get very different geohashes. They lie in different halves of the world. A bounding-box search between the southwest and northeast corner geohashes retrieves every point along the Z-order curve between them, which can be far too many. Even so, geohashing has been used for proximity search in MongoDB, HBase and Accumulo.

sysd-reliab-007.title: Nearby search with a quadtree: walking down to the origin
sysd-reliab-007.text: A location service finds nearby businesses by walking down a tree. The quadtree is an in-memory data structure, not a data store, built on each server when it starts. The root is the whole world map, divided into 4 quadrants until no node has more than 100 businesses. To search, walk from the root to the leaf holding the origin. If it has 100 businesses, return it; otherwise add businesses from its neighbors. Building a quadtree for 200 million businesses may take a few minutes, during which the server cannot serve traffic. New releases roll out to a few servers at a time to avoid a brownout.

openers.blocks: Every large system is assembled from smaller parts that each do one job well. This part gathers those building blocks, and it begins with the smallest: algorithms and data structures. A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, a hash collision happens when two distinct pieces of data share one, and a Bloom filter tests whether an element is in a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives. Trees such as the quadtree, k-d tree and trie, and curves such as the Z-order and Hilbert curves, organize space and strings so they can be searched. Later chapters build on them with load balancing, proxies, caching and storage.
openers.algorithms-behind-the-systems: Behind the big boxes in a system diagram sit small ideas from computer science. A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, and a hash collision is what happens when two distinct pieces of data share one. Base64 lets binary data travel over channels that carry only text, and MD5 is a widely used hash function that produces a 128-bit value. The chapter then turns to space and strings: the quadtree, the k-d tree and the trie, curves such as the Z-order and the Hilbert curve, and geohash, which encodes latitude and longitude as a short string. Along the way it meets the Bloom filter, which tests set membership with false positives but never false negatives, and similarity hashing, which shows when data is similar but not identical.

reviews.algorithms-behind-the-systems: Hash functions turn up almost everywhere in this chapter. They index data, they sit inside Bloom filters, Merkle trees, count-min sketches and HyperLogLog, and they build name-based UUIDs. Because collisions are certain, the structures built on them either tolerate collisions, as the Bloom filter does with false positives, or maximize them on purpose, as similarity hashing does. The second thread is space: quadtrees, k-d trees, the Z-order and Hilbert curves, and geohash all turn locations into something that can be searched, and the limits show up near borders for geohash and in many dimensions for the k-d tree. The third thread is naming, from UUID versions to Snowflake IDs, which trade sortability, size and coordination against one another.
